input: The compressor casing wall thickness stands at 68 mm once the corrosion allowance has been added, and it is the discharge condition that ultimately governs the thickness, since the discharge side is exposed to the higher pressure at the higher temperature. The margin embodied in the 68 mm is precisely the margin on which the absorber design already relies, given that the discharge line runs directly to the absorber, and any reduction in wall thickness at this location would effectively relocate the weak point of the train to the one connection that cannot be isolated while the lean solvent pump remains in operation. During a trip, the casing is exposed to the full discharge $\Delta P$ under blocked-outlet conditions, when the machine continues to run against a closed discharge and the pressure at the casing reaches its highest credible level. Turning to the sealing arrangements, the two gasket materials that have been carried forward are to be compared strictly on the basis of temperature limit, and on that criterion the higher-rated material is clearly to be preferred, since it maintains its seal at the discharge temperature with a comfortable margin to spare, whereas the lower-rated material sits sufficiently close to its limit that a single hot excursion during a trip could age it in one event. Chemical resistance does not meaningfully separate the two candidates, as both are offered for the same solvent service, and at a joint of this size cost does not separate them either. The higher-rated material is accordingly preferred for the discharge joint, and the same stock is preferred for the suction joint as well, so that a single gasket specification can be held for the machine as a whole. On the suction side, the joint experiences the conditions delivered by the lean solvent pump, and it should be noted that the NPSH margin available at that pump is in no way affected by the gasket selection.
